title: Choose a partner by faith, not by what dazzles you.
subtitle: What a marriage invites you toward
then: Ibn Kathir notes this verse put {idea}a believing servant above a free, wealthy idolater{/idea}, even an impressive one. He cites the hadith: a woman is chosen for wealth, status, beauty and religion, so {reward}choose the one with religion{/reward}. A spouse shapes where your heart is pulled.
now: The profile with the perfect photos and the great job. The family pushing someone because of their surname. {trap}Impressive can still pull you away from Allah.{/trap} The person you share a home with shapes your prayers, your kids, your Ramadan.
old: If they are attractive and successful, the rest will work itself out.
new: The best partner is the one who pulls me toward Allah, even if they impress me less.
try: Write down the three qualities you most want in a spouse, or value in yours. Is faith on the list?

title: A time of discomfort, not a reason to shut her out.
subtitle: Respect for the body without pushing people away
then: Anas reported some people in Madinah would {trap}not eat with or even mingle with women{/trap} during their period. The Companions asked and this verse came. Aisha described the Prophet ﷺ {idea}resting his head in her lap reciting Qur'an{/idea}, and drinking from the cup where she had drunk.
now: Your sister is curled up with cramps and someone in the house treats her like she is dirty. Or you feel awkward and keep away. {idea}Tenderness is the sunnah here.{/idea} Bring the hot water bottle, sit with her, share the meal.
old: During her period, it is respectful to keep away from her.
new: One boundary is set, but closeness, care, and shared meals stay.
try: Do one caring thing today for a woman in your home who is not feeling well.

title: Even your private life is planting for your meeting with Allah.
subtitle: Intimacy, offspring, and what you send ahead
then: Jabir reported that {trap}a superstition about marriage{/trap} was being spread in Madinah, and this verse answered it. Ibn Abbas explained the field as the place of pregnancy. The verse closes not with permission alone, but with {idea}send good ahead, fear Allah, and know you will meet Him{/idea}.
now: Marriage has its private side, and no one else sees it. {idea}Kindness, patience, and care there are deeds too.{/idea} The children who may come, the way you treat each other behind the closed door, all of it is sent ahead.
old: What happens between spouses has nothing to do with my faith.
new: Even the most private part of my marriage is seen by Allah and can be good I send ahead.
try: Make a short dua today for your spouse or future spouse, and for righteous children.

title: Do not use Allah's name to lock yourself out of doing good.
subtitle: Oaths that block kindness

row.title: keep my word at all costs

then: Ibn Kathir explains the verse as {trap}swearing by Allah to stop doing good{/trap}, like cutting off relatives. He cites the Prophet ﷺ: when I swear to something and see something better, {idea}I do what is better{/idea}. He also cites 24:22, where the generous are told not to swear off helping kin.
now: After the wedding argument you told your brother, wallahi I am done with you. Now he needs help moving and you are stuck behind your own words. {idea}Allah never asked you to use His name as a wall against good.{/idea}
old: I swore it, so now I have to stick to cutting them off.
new: Allah's name is not a tool for my grudges, and choosing the better thing honors Him more.
try: Think of something you swore off in anger. Ask someone with knowledge how to make it right.

title: Allah looks at what your heart meant, not habit words.
subtitle: Slips of the tongue versus intentions
then: Aisha reported the Prophet ﷺ described the unintended oath as {idea}a man at home saying, no by Allah, yes by Allah{/idea}. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said what is held to account is {trap}swearing while knowing you lie{/trap}. Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.
now: You say wallahi ten times a day without thinking. Then once, to get out of trouble at work, you say it knowing it is false. {trap}That one is different.{/trap} Allah is gentle with the habit, serious about the heart.
old: Words are words; swearing is no big deal either way.
new: Allah forgives my careless habits, but what my heart knowingly does is mine to carry.
try: Notice today how often you swear by Allah. Try saying yes or no on its own.

title: Withdrawing from a spouse cannot become an endless punishment.
subtitle: A limit on silent treatment in marriage
then: Ibn Kathir explains the old practice of a husband {trap}swearing off his wife{/trap}, leaving her neither married in practice nor free. The verse sets a limit so that, in his words, {idea}the wife is not harmed{/idea}. If he returns, Allah is {reward}Forgiving and Merciful{/reward} for what was neglected.
now: Days of not speaking. Sleeping on the sofa to make a point. Phone on silent when they call. {trap}Withdrawal can become a weapon.{/trap} The verse puts a fence around it: you do not get to leave someone hanging forever.
old: Going cold on my spouse is a fair way to show how hurt I am.
new: My hurt is real, but leaving someone suspended harms them, and the door back stays open.
try: If you are in a cold patch with someone close, send one warm message today.

title: If you decide to part, Allah hears and knows how.
subtitle: Making the hard decision in full view of Allah

row.title: Hearing, Knowing
sub: He sees how you do it

row.title: once it is over, it is private

then: Ibn Kathir notes from Ibn Umar and many Companions that {idea}a decision has to actually be made{/idea}: return, or part. The verse does not end with a threat but with two names: {idea}All-Hearing, All-Knowing{/idea}. Every word spoken in that decision is heard.
now: The lawyer's office. The family meeting where everyone talks over each other. The messages you send the ex at midnight. {idea}Allah hears all of it.{/idea} Even an ending can be done with dignity.
old: Once a marriage is ending, how I behave does not really matter.
new: Allah hears how I part as much as how I stayed, so I can end things with dignity.
try: If you are in a hard family conflict, reread your last message before sending the next one.

title: Be honest in hard moments. Both spouses have rights.
subtitle: Truthfulness, a pause, and fairness
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah left women {idea}trusted as the authority on what only they know{/idea}, and warned against hiding it. A return is for those who {reward}want to set things right{/reward}. Ibn Abbas said: I groom myself for my wife as I like her to for me, because {idea}they have rights like those upon them{/idea}.
now: You expect your spouse to look after themselves, be patient, keep their word. Do you do the same? {idea}The verse puts both of you under the same standard of fairness.{/idea} Even in a breakup, telling the truth is still worship.
old: In marriage I mostly think about what I am owed.
new: What I expect from my spouse is the measure of what I owe them.
try: Do one thing today for your spouse or a family member that you usually expect from them.
